cards.text: Psalm 119 keeps going, and the psalmist is still talking straight to the LORD: "Remember Your word to Your servant, upon which You have given me hope." Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer hoping somebody would remember ME, so this man has my full attention.

cards.question: The psalmist is in the middle of affliction. What does he say is his comfort in it?

answers.text: God's promise has given him life
His enemies have finally gone quiet
His friends have stayed close by

cards.text: But the hard times have company. He says, "The arrogant utterly deride me." UTTERLY, friend, that's not a side comment in the group chat, that's a full roast.

cards.question: True or false: with the arrogant mocking him, the psalmist turns away from God's law.

cards.text: Mocked on one side and afflicted on the other, he needs comfort from somewhere. So he looks back.

cards.question: When the psalmist looks back for comfort, what does he remember?

cards.text: Then the mood flips. Comfort is out, and rage takes hold of him.

cards.question: Rage takes hold of the psalmist because of the wicked who ___ God's law.

cards.text: Now he paints a picture of his life. It's a pilgrimage, and he's a traveler just passing through.

cards.question: On his pilgrimage, the psalmist says God's statutes are ___ to him.

cards.text: A road trip playlist, and every track is God's statutes. Then night falls, and the psalmist's mind is still on the LORD.

cards.question: True or false: in the night, the psalmist remembers the LORD's name so that he may keep God's law.
The psalmist calls remembering the LORD this way his practice. What reason does he give?

cards.text: Next stretch, and the psalmist makes a big claim: "The LORD is my portion." His share is the LORD Himself, friend, and that's not the biggest cookie on the tray, that's the WHOLE BAKERY.

cards.question: With the LORD as his portion, what has the psalmist promised?

cards.text: Then he says, "I have sought Your face with all my heart." And right behind it comes a request.

cards.question: The psalmist asks God to be ___ to him according to His promise.

cards.text: Then he takes an honest look at himself: he considered his ways. The last time I considered MY ways, friend, I was in the back of a junk drawer, and it took about two seconds.

cards.question: After considering his ways, where does the psalmist turn his steps?
True or false: once he turned, the psalmist took his time before keeping God's commandments.

cards.text: No snooze button on this man. Then he says that even though the ropes of the wicked bind him, there's something he holds on to.

cards.question: Even though the ropes of the wicked bind him, the psalmist ___ God's law.

cards.text: Most people sleep through the night. Not this man, and friend, at midnight the only thing getting ME out of bed is the oven timer.

cards.question: At midnight the psalmist rises. What for?

cards.text: He's careful about the company he keeps, too.

cards.question: Who does the psalmist say he is a friend to?

answers.text: Anyone who is kind to him

cards.question: True or false: the psalmist says the earth is filled with the LORD's loving devotion.

cards.text: Last stretch, and it opens on a good note: "You are good to Your servant, O LORD, according to Your word." Then the psalmist asks God to teach him good judgment and knowledge.

cards.question: True or false: the psalmist asks God to teach him good judgment because he believes in God's commandments.
The psalmist gets honest about his past. Before he was afflicted, what does he say he did?

cards.text: But now he keeps God's word, and he tells the LORD, "You are good, and You do what is good; teach me Your statutes."
Then the arrogant are back, and this time they've smeared him with lies.

cards.question: True or false: after the arrogant smear him with lies, the psalmist pulls back from God's precepts.

cards.text: He says their hearts are callous and insensitive. That's dough left out overnight, friend: you poke it and NOTHING gives.

cards.question: Their hearts are callous, but the psalmist ___ in God's law.

cards.text: Then comes the most surprising line in this whole stretch. He looks back at his affliction and says it was good for him.

cards.question: Why does the psalmist say it was good for him to be afflicted?

answers.text: So he might learn God's statutes
So his enemies would leave him
So he could rest from his work

cards.question: The psalmist ends by weighing the law from God's mouth against riches. What does he say the law is more precious than?

answers.text: Thousands of pieces of gold and silver
A king's crown and his throne

cards.text: Thousands of pieces of gold and silver, and friend, I left a closing-sale bin with a 25 cent sticker on me, so God's law and I are NOT in the same price range. That's where we'll stop for now, but this psalm is far from finished.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 3 quotes "The arrogant utterly deride me.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 1 quotes "The LORD is my portion.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 3 quotes "I have sought Your face with all my heart.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: "He needs comfort from somewhere. So he looks back" gives a reason for why the psalmist remembers God's judgments. Psalm 119:52 only says he remembers them and finds comfort in them. It never says he remembers them because he needs comfort.

rule.text: Reasons: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: "Comfort is out" claims the comfort of 119:52 has ended when rage takes hold in 119:53. The text never connects the two verses this way or says his comfort is gone.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question says the psalmist calls "remembering the LORD this way" his practice. Psalm 119:56 only says "This is my practice" and never says what "this" refers to. The card ties it to verse 55.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answers "silent" and "distant" aren't believable. Nobody who has just sought God's face with all his heart would ask God to be silent or distant to him according to His promise, so "gracious" stands out.

rule.text: Wrong answers for what someone does or says only need to be believable.

findings.problem: The joke "I was in the back of a junk drawer, and it took about two seconds" doesn't click. It's unclear why considering his ways in the drawer would take two seconds, so the punchline needs explaining.

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining.

findings.problem: The setup says "there's something he holds on to," which rules out the wrong answers "resents" and "ignores" on card 9 and leaves only "remembers."

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "He's careful about the company he keeps" rules out the wrong answers on card 13 ("Anyone who is kind to him," "Everyone in his town"). Psalm 119:63 also never says he is careful about his company.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "He kept God's law" is true elsewhere in the passage. In 119:67 he says "now I keep Your word," and verses 56, 57 and 69 say the same kind of thing. It's only false for the time before he was afflicted.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: The question begins "Their hearts are callous" without saying who "their" is. The arrogant were only named on story cards 5 and 7, which are no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: This true or false (the arrogant smear him with lies, does he pull back from God's precepts) asks the same thing as stop 1 card 4 (the arrogant mock him, does he turn from God's law). The baker can answer it from the earlier pattern. The verses aren't the same line, so the refrain rule doesn't apply.
findings.question: Should Prep avoid asking a near-identical question about two different verses that make the same point, or is the repetition fine since it follows the psalm's own repetition?
